parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: moment as turning effect of a force
hints: Hint 1: Think about what makes a turning effect larger - a bigger push helps, but so does pushing further from the pivot and pushing at right angles to the object.
parts.proper_answer: Moment of a force = force $\times$ perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the point (pivot).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a Moment Measures**
Imagine pushing a door open. Pushing hard near the handle works well, but pushing near the hinges does almost nothing. So a moment is the turning effect, and it depends on two things together: how big the force $F$ is, and how far from the pivot you apply it.

Step 2: **Why Perpendicular Matters**
Only the part of the distance that is at $90^{\circ}$ to the force causes turning. So we always use the shortest, perpendicular distance $d$ from the pivot to the line of the force. In symbols: $$ \text{moment} = F \times d_{\perp} $$

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: clockwise and anticlockwise moments about same point
hints: Hint 1: Start by recalling the condition for no overall turning - the object must be balanced rotationally, not spinning up in either direction.
Hint 2: Think about how to compare the two turning directions fairly - they must be calculated about the same pivot point for the balance to make sense.
parts.proper_answer: For a body in (rotational) equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Condition for No Turning**
If the trapdoor is held still at $42^{\circ}$ it is not rotating. That means it is in rotational equilibrium, so the total turning effect in one sense must exactly cancel the total turning effect in the opposite sense.

Step 2: **Balancing About the Same Point**
Moments depend on where you take the pivot, so you must add up all clockwise moments and all anticlockwise moments about the same point, for example hinge A. Equilibrium means: $$ \sum M_{clockwise} = \sum M_{anticlockwise} $$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Sketch the vertical 75 N weight at the centre and the trapdoor at $42^{\circ}$ to the horizontal - look for the small right-angled triangle that gives the part at $90^{\circ}$ to the door.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Only the Perpendicular Part Turns**
Weight acts straight down, but the trapdoor is tilted at $42^{\circ}$. The component along the door just pulls through the hinge and causes no moment. Only the component at $90^{\circ}$ to the door causes a moment about A.

Step 2: **Resolving With Cosine**
From the geometry, the angle between the vertical weight and the perpendicular to the door is $42^{\circ}$. So the perpendicular component is adjacent to that angle: $$ W_{\perp} = W \cos 42^{\circ} = 75 \times \cos 42^{\circ} $$ $$ W_{\perp} = 56\text{ N} $$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
key_concepts: weight acting at centre of uniform rod
hints: Hint 1: Focus on hinge A as the pivot - the weight acts at the middle of the uniform 80 cm door, while $F$ acts at the far end B, both perpendicular to the door.
Hint 2: Set the anticlockwise moment due to $F$ equal to the clockwise moment due to the perpendicular component of weight, then solve for $F$.
parts.proper_answer: Taking moments about A: $F \times 80 = 56 \times 40$, so $F = 28\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the Pivot and Distances**
Take moments about hinge A so the unknown hinge force has no moment. The door is uniform, so its 75 N weight acts at its centre, $40\text{ cm}$ from A. Force $F$ acts at end B, $80\text{ cm}$ from A. Both forces are now considered perpendicular to the door, so distance along the door can be used directly.

Step 2: **Equate Opposite Moments**
$F$ tries to turn the door anticlockwise, the perpendicular component of weight tries to turn it clockwise. In equilibrium: $$ F \times 80 = 55.7 \times 40 $$ $$ F = \frac{55.7 \times 40}{80} = 28\text{ N} $$
